title: Backflow preventer diagram: RPZ, double check, and PVB parts
description: Read labeled RPZ, double-check and PVB diagrams. Compare manufacturer parts drawings, cover layouts and real project constraints before choosing a leak or service path.
prompt: What can the assembly layout tell me without becoming a remote diagnosis?
answer: A diagram helps label visible zones such as shutoffs, test cocks, checks, relief or vent paths, and unions. It does not establish the model, hazard classification, part compatibility, or repair method.
urgency: Use diagrams only for observation and communication. Escalate any active discharge, damage, failed test, or uncertain device identity.
diagramAlt: Conceptual RPZ assembly; compare the labeled RPZ, double-check and PVB drawings below
identifiers: The manufacturer label identifies the product; the diagram only describes a device family.
Visible ports and covers can help communicate a leak location to a technician.
System use and local requirements cannot be inferred from a simplified drawing.

steps.body: Take a full-device photo and identify visible components without disassembly.

steps.title: Close the risk loop
steps.body: Route to model-specific service, testing, or installation requirements based on verified identity.

safeChecks: Do not use a drawing to select a repair kit.
Do not adjust screws or test ports based on a diagram.
Keep safety and access boundaries visible in photos.
Photograph the model suffix, nominal size and flow arrow, then open the matching manufacturer drawing.
Separate a parts drawing, a dimensional drawing and an installation detail in the service brief.

fieldSections.title: Read the parts before choosing a service path.
fieldSections.introduction: These sketches describe device families. Record the actual label and photograph the complete assembly plus the suspected leak point.

rows.meaning: They isolate the assembly for qualified service; their position does not prove the checks pass.
rows.nextStep: Keep shutoff access clear and record flow direction.

rows.meaning: Covers provide service access; test cocks support field testing. External wetness and an internal failed check are different evidence.
rows.nextStep: Give the technician the exact wet location and failed-test report.

rows.meaning: The relief path distinguishes an RPZ from a double-check assembly. Discharge needs investigation and a suitable drainage route.
rows.nextStep: Keep the outlet open; use the RPZ leak path.

rows.meaning: A PVB has an atmospheric air inlet and a different installation and leakage pattern.

fieldSections.title: Double-check diagram: two checks do not mean two covers.
fieldSections.introduction: The Watts 007 has one service cover over two checks. The Wilkins 350XL uses a different removable housing. Cover count alone cannot identify the assembly.

rows.meaning: Two check modules beneath one cover, with a cover O-ring and separate test connections.
rows.nextStep: See the exploded service view on PDF page 3.

rows.meaning: The parts sheet distinguishes body, housing, inlet/outlet housing O-rings and checks.
rows.nextStep: Use PDF page 2 for the exploded drawing and page 1 for the matching size column.

rows.observation: Water below an assumed double check
rows.meaning: A DCVA has no RPZ differential relief outlet. Wet housing joints or test ports are a different observation.
rows.nextStep: Recheck the label and use the double-check leak guide.

fieldSections.caption: Original conceptual single-cover example, not a universal casting or port layout. Dashed checks are internal; use the exact model drawing.

fieldSections.title: PVB diagram: one check and an atmospheric air inlet.
fieldSections.introduction: A pressure vacuum breaker has a different flow path from an RPZ. The FEBCO 765 drawing separates canopy, bonnet, poppet and check assembly; similar names do not make their parts interchangeable.

rows.meaning: The bonnet/poppet is above the check assembly; the parts table has separate nominal-size columns.
rows.nextStep: Open the exploded view on PDF page 5; use the observed model and size.

rows.meaning: An intentional air opening is not the same location as a cracked bonnet or threaded fitting.
rows.nextStep: Use timing and location in the vacuum-breaker guide.

rows.meaning: A parts view identifies components. It does not specify the approved site elevation, drainage or hazard protection.
rows.nextStep: Use the installation detail guide for model-specific placement.

caseStudies.title: Brenham Hospital: a diagram needs site measurements
caseStudies.constraint: Existing piping and a confined mechanical room limited replacement options.
caseStudies.documentedAction: Watts reports that measurements informed the selection of a 957 RPZ.
caseStudies.planningLesson: Match the exact drawing to the actual space and service access. A family sketch does not establish fit or approval.

questions.question: What are the main parts of a backflow preventer?
questions.answer: Match the device family first. An RPZ has two checks and a differential relief path; a DCVA has two checks without that relief valve; a PVB has one check and an atmospheric air inlet. Shutoffs, test connections and service covers vary by model.

questions.question: Does every double-check assembly have two covers?
questions.answer: No. The Watts 007 service drawing shows two checks under one cover. The number or shape of covers is not enough to identify a model or select replacement parts.

questions.question: Which drawing should I use to find replacement parts?
questions.answer: Use the manufacturer’s exploded parts drawing and its matching size/revision table. Installation views show placement; dimension tables show fit; simplified family drawings show function. None substitutes for a verified service diagnosis.

questions.question: Can a diagram tell whether a check valve has failed?
questions.answer: A drawing identifies the intended components and path. Internal check performance requires the appropriate field test; a photograph or dry exterior cannot establish a passing result.

questions.question: Where is the leak opening on the diagram?
questions.answer: Compare the RPZ relief outlet, PVB bonnet/air inlet, and DCVA cover, housing joints or test connections. Photograph the full device and the exact wet point, then follow the corresponding symptom guide.
